nameStory: Prairie smoke gets its enchanting name from the wispy, feathery seed heads that appear after flowering, creating silvery plumes that dance in the wind like wisps of smoke rising from the prairie. The alternative name "old man's whiskers" comes from these same feathery appendages, which look remarkably like a grandfather's flowing white beard swaying in the breeze.
description: Prairie smoke is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms small clumps close to the ground. The plant produces nodding, bell-shaped flowers in spring that hang downward like tiny lanterns, followed by its famous feathery seed plumes that can reach 1-2 feet tall. This member of the rose family is extremely rare in New England, typically staying under a foot tall with deeply divided, fernlike leaves.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Long, silky-white feathery plumes up to 2 inches long create dramatic wispy clusters that catch sunlight and blow in the wind like ethereal smoke

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pinkish to purplish bell-shaped flowers that nod downward, usually appearing in groups of three (hence "three-flowered avens")

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fernlike leaves that feel soft and are arranged in a basal rosette close to the ground, with smaller leaves on flowering stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, clumping perennial that hugs the ground with most leaves in a rosette, sending up slender flowering stalks in spring

habitat: Prairie smoke is exceptionally rare in New England, found only in isolated populations in dry, rocky soils or prairie-like openings. Look for it in well-drained, sunny spots with thin soils, possibly on rocky slopes or in areas that mimic the drier western conditions where it's more common.

seasonality.spring: Nodding pinkish flowers bloom in late spring, followed quickly by the development of the characteristic feathery seed plumes that make identification unmistakable.
seasonality.summer: The dramatic silvery-white feathery seed heads are at their peak, creating the "smoke" effect this plant is famous for while seeds disperse on the wind.
seasonality.fall: Basal leaves may take on reddish tints before dying back, while old seed stalks may persist as brown remnants.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and the underground perennial root system to survive until spring.

funFact: Prairie smoke is like a botanical time traveler - it's actually a relic species from the last ice age that got stranded in tiny New England populations when the climate warmed and its preferred cold, dry prairie habitat retreated westward thousands of years ago.
confusionNotes: The feathery seed heads are so distinctive that prairie smoke is unlikely to be confused with anything else when in seed. In flower, it might be mistaken for other avens species, but the nodding, pinkish bells and the basal rosette of finely divided leaves help distinguish it.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - prairie smoke in New England isn't found in prairies since we don't have true prairies here. Instead, look for it in the rare dry, open habitats that most closely mimic the western prairie conditions where this plant thrives.
compareHints: Unlike other New England avens which typically have upward-facing yellow or white flowers, prairie smoke has distinctive nodding pinkish flowers and creates the dramatic feathery seed plumes that no other regional avens species produce. Water avens also nods but has larger, darker flowers and lacks the spectacular plumed seeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's avens species, white avens is distinguished by its small white petals and grabby seed heads.
Water Avens stands out among its relatives by being the wetland specialist with drooping flowers.
Unlike its avens relatives that grow in woodlands and meadows, Eastern Mountain Avens is the only species in its genus adapted to extreme alpine conditions in New England.
Among New England's avens species, yellow avens is the most common and widespread.
Rough avens is the scruffiest member of the New England avens family, with the most noticeably hairy and rough-textured leaves.
Among New England's avens, Large-leaved Avens is the champion of seed dispersal with its aggressively clingy fruit balls.
Wood Avens differs from our native White Avens by having yellow flowers instead of white ones and preferring shadier spots.
Among New England's avens species, Spring Avens stands out for its early bloom time and preference for consistently moist, rich soils.

Among New England's avens species, cream-colored avens stands out for its distinctly pale yellow to cream flowers - white avens has pure white petals, yellow avens has bright yellow ones, and water avens has drooping, bell-shaped flowers.

Scarlet Avens stands out dramatically from all other New England avens species primarily due to its bright red flowers - our native avens species like White Avens, Water Avens, and Yellow Avens all have much more subdued flower colors.
